title: Broadcasting Internet Datagrams
summary: This RFC proposes simple rules for broadcasting Internet datagrams on local networks that support broadcast, for addressing such broadcasts, and for how gateways should treat them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 919 defines how IP can address a datagram to all hosts on a network. It also sets gateway rules that prevent the same broadcast from circulating around a network.

questions: how should gateways handle broadcast datagrams
how do gateways avoid broadcast loops
how do gateways prevent broadcast loops
subtitle: Rules for sending an IP datagram to every host on a local or remote network.

tldr.problem: The basic IP specification did not define a common way to address broadcasts or explain how gateways should forward them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 919 reserves an all-ones host number for broadcast and tells gateways never to rebroadcast a datagram on the hardware network where it arrived.
tldr.outcome: RFC 919 is an Internet Standard that defines local and directed broadcast behavior. It warns that each broadcast consumes work on every host that hears it.

facts.label: Forwarding
facts.value: Local all-ones address must not be forwarded

today: RFC 919 is an Internet Standard published in October 1984. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; RFC 919 refers readers to RFC 922 for subnet interactions.

sections.title: Why Broadcasts Are Useful and Costly
sections.content:
A broadcast reaches all neighboring hosts without requiring the sender to know which one has the needed information. A host can also use one to announce information to many neighbors. This is useful for tasks such as discovering gateways or reaching name and time servers.

RFC 919 covers unreliable, unsequenced datagrams that may be duplicated. It assumes the local data-link layer supports efficient broadcast, but it does not guarantee delivery. Every host that hears a broadcast spends effort on it, so the RFC says to use broadcasts only when they are the best solution.
sections.plainLanguage: A broadcast can reach an unknown host quickly, but every host on the network must handle it. Use one only when sending to a known individual would not solve the problem.

sections.title: Four Broadcast Classes
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes four cases: a link-layer broadcast carrying an IP datagram for one host; a broadcast to all hosts on the local IP network; a directed broadcast to all hosts on a remote IP network; and a broadcast to the entire Internet. The first case is not an IP broadcast because the IP destination still names one host.

A directed broadcast is routed normally until it reaches a gateway attached to the target network, where the gateway broadcasts it locally. The RFC considers an Internet-wide broadcast probably useless and undesirable. Gateways may refuse to forward broadcasts for performance or security reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: A broadcast can target one local recipient at the link layer, every host on a local network, every host on a remote network, or the whole Internet. The RFC treats the last option as undesirable.

sections.title: Broadcast Address Notation
sections.content:
RFC 919 assigns the all-ones value to the host-number part of an IP address to mean all hosts. The address 255.255.255.255 means a broadcast on the local hardware network and MUST NOT be forwarded. A host on network 36 can use 36.255.255.255 to address all hosts on network 36.

For comparison, 36.0.0.0 is notation for network 36, not a broadcast to its hosts. Without subnets, the local hardware broadcast and the broadcast to all of network 36 have the same effect.
sections.plainLanguage: All ones in the host part means every host in the named network. The special all-ones address 255.255.255.255 stays on the local hardware network.

sections.title: Host Processing
sections.content:
A host that receives IP broadcasts must compare the destination address with both its own addresses and the broadcast addresses that apply to it. Without broadcast support, its IP layer normally checks only whether the destination matches one of the host's own addresses.

A sender needs no special IP procedure: it supplies the appropriate destination address and sends the datagram as usual. The RFC assumes the data-link layer handles the local broadcast operation.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiving host must recognize both its own address and the broadcast address for its network. A sender uses the broadcast destination like any other IP destination.

sections.title: Gateway Rules Prevent Broadcast Loops
sections.content:
A gateway must never broadcast a datagram on the same hardware network where it received that datagram. Merely avoiding broadcasts that the gateway sent itself is not enough when several gateways share a network.

If a broadcast has reached its target hardware network, the gateway does not forward it again but may treat itself as a destination. If the target is another connected network, it sends a link-layer broadcast there. Otherwise it uses normal routing to choose the next gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway must not repeat a broadcast back onto the network where it heard it. That rule prevents neighboring gateways from repeating the same datagram indefinitely.

sections.title: ARP Must Not Resolve Broadcast Addresses
sections.content:
An ARP server should never answer a request whose target is an IP broadcast address. The request may come from a host that does not recognize the broadcast address. Answering it could cause forwarding loops.

The RFC warns that if multiple hosts misunderstand the address, a datagram with Time-To-Live T could produce as many as T**N spurious rebroadcasts, where N is the number of such hosts. The document leaves subnet interactions to RFC 922.
sections.plainLanguage: An ARP server must not turn a broadcast address into a hardware destination. Doing so can make hosts and gateways repeat a broadcast many times.
